steps.title: Find the office that holds each record
steps.detail: Birth certificates come from the vital records office of the state where you were born; marriage certificates from the state or, in some states, the county where the licence was issued. The CDC keeps the directory for every state, with addresses, fees and whether you can order online.

steps.title: Order the long-form certified copy
steps.detail: Ask for the certified, long-form (sometimes "vault" or "full") copy with the raised or embossed seal, not the short abstract or a wallet card. Apostille offices refuse photocopies and notarised copies; consulates like a copy issued within the last six months.

steps.title: Order two of each
steps.detail: One goes off for the apostille and stays in the French file for years; the second is your spare. Ordering later from France is slow.

steps.title: Check the copy when it arrives
steps.detail: Names spelled exactly as in the passport, the seal present, the registrar's signature legible. A record with a discrepancy is the one that gets refused in France.

bring: Parents' names and the place and date of the event, for the order form
Order certified copies of your civil rec.time: A few days to four weeks, depending on the state and whether you order online or by post.
Order certified copies of your civil rec.cost: Usually $10 to $35 per copy, plus a processing fee for online orders.

links.label: Where to write for vital records (CDC)

steps.title: Find the apostille office for North Carolina
steps.detail: Each state's Secretary of State (or equivalent) apostilles the records that state issued. The National Association of Secretaries of State keeps the directory: office, fee, mail or walk-in, current turnaround.

steps.title: Check whether a county step comes first
steps.detail: In a few states a record signed by a county or city registrar must be certified by the county clerk before the state will apostille it. The state's apostille page says so; the CDC directory notes it for vital records.

steps.title: Send or bring the certified copy with the request form
steps.detail: The original certified copy, the state's apostille request form naming France as the destination country, the fee, and a prepaid return envelope if by mail. Never send a photocopy.

steps.title: Keep the apostille attached
steps.detail: The apostille is a stapled or glued page. Do not remove it, and do not laminate anything. Scan the whole thing front and back once it comes home; the scan is what the translator and, later, French offices work from.

bring: The certified copy of each record
Get the apostilles from the state.time: One to three weeks in most states; some offer same-day counter service, others take four or more by mail.
Get the apostilles from the state.cost: Roughly $5 to $40 per document, set by the state.

links.label: Where to write for vital records (CDC)

steps.title: Know what the consulate is checking
steps.detail: Cover for the full visa period, at least €30,000 for medical costs, repatriation included, no exclusion for pre-existing conditions, valid in France. Ordinary travel insurance and US domestic plans are refused.

steps.title: Compare expatriate policies
steps.detail: Insurers who sell "visa long séjour" or "expatriate" policies issue an attestation written for French consulates, in French or English, with the dates and the amounts on it. That letter is the document; the policy booklet is not.

steps.title: Buy for the visa dates, cancellable
steps.detail: Cover should start on the day the visa starts. Once French health cover opens after three months of residence you can cut it back or cancel, so look for a policy that allows it.

steps.title: Print the attestation
steps.detail: One per applicant, each named. It goes in the dossier and travels with you.

Buy health insurance for the whole first.time: A day or two to arrange; the letter is usually immediate.
Buy health insurance for the whole first.cost: Varies with age and cover; budget from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars a year.

steps.title: Choose the kind of proof
steps.detail: A signed lease, a deed, a hotel or rental booking for the first weeks, or an attestation d'hébergement from a host in France with a copy of their ID and a recent utility bill.

steps.title: Check what your consulate accepts
steps.detail: The France-Visas wizard lists the accepted proofs for your route; most US consulates accept a booking covering the first weeks.

steps.title: Get it in writing, dated
steps.detail: A booking confirmation with your name, the address and the dates; a lease signed by both sides; a host letter signed and dated.

bring: The booking, lease or host attestation with the host's ID and utility bill
Line up where you will live for the firs.time: A day for a booking; weeks for a lease at a distance.

steps.title: Ask for French visa photos, not US passport photos
steps.detail: French specification: 35 x 45 mm, taken within six months, plain light grey or white background, neutral expression, no glasses glare. A US 2 x 2 inch photo is the wrong size and gets rejected at the counter.

steps.title: Get several
steps.detail: Two go in the dossier; keep spares for the validation and the residence card later. TLScontact centres sell them too, for a fee.

steps.title: Say who you are and why France
steps.detail: One page, dated and signed. Where you will live, for how long, how you support yourself, and what you will do with your time. For a couple, each writes their own or both sign one.

steps.title: Match the file
steps.detail: Every figure and date in the letter must agree with the documents behind it: the same address as the accommodation proof, the same income as the statements.

steps.title: Let the portal draft it
steps.detail: Documents has a draft written for your route from your profile. Check every line, print it, sign and date it.

steps.title: French or English
steps.detail: US consulates accept English. A short French version alongside is a courtesy, not a requirement.

steps.title: Download official statements for the last three months
steps.detail: From each account you are relying on: checking, savings, investment. Official PDFs with the bank's name, your name and the account number, not screenshots.

steps.title: Add the proof of income
steps.detail: Pay slips or an employer letter, the Social Security award letter, pension statements, a rental income ledger: whatever shows the money keeps coming.

steps.title: Date it to the appointment
steps.detail: Statements older than three months get asked for again. Pull them in the last two weeks before the appointment and add a fresh balance printout on the day.

bring: Statements from every account you rely on
Pull three months of bank statements.cost: Nothing; some banks charge for stamped copies.

steps.title: Create the account and run the wizard
steps.detail: On france-visas.gouv.fr, answer with your real nationality, country of residence, purpose of stay and length. The wizard tells you the visa category and produces the document list for your route.

steps.title: Fill in the long-stay form
steps.detail: One application per adult; children are separate applications too. Save as you go. Spelling of names and passport numbers exactly as in the passport.

steps.title: Print, sign, keep the receipt
steps.detail: The signed form and the receipt page with the France-Visas reference number are the first two things checked at the appointment.

bring: Details of your accommodation in France

steps.title: Create the TLScontact account
steps.detail: TLScontact has run French visa intake in the US since April 2025. Link your France-Visas reference to the account.

steps.title: Pick any of the ten centres
steps.detail: New York, Boston, Washington, Atlanta, Miami, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, San Francisco or Seattle; you are not tied to the one nearest you. Slots open a few weeks ahead and go fast from May to August.

steps.title: Book everyone on the same day
steps.detail: A couple or a family books consecutive slots so the files travel together.

steps.title: Pay the service fee online
steps.detail: About €220 per long-stay applicant, charged in dollars, non-refundable. Optional extras (priority slot, courier return) change comfort, not the decision.

Book the TLScontact appointment.time: Twenty minutes; the wait for a slot is what takes time.
Book the TLScontact appointment.cost: About €220 service fee per long-stay applicant.

steps.title: Order the file the way the list reads
steps.detail: Follow the France-Visas document list top to bottom: originals in one pile, one photocopy of each in another. Missing pieces mean the file goes home and you rebook.

steps.title: Arrive early with everyone applying
steps.detail: Each applicant appears in person, children included. Fingerprints and a photo are taken for everyone over twelve.

steps.title: Pay the visa fee
steps.detail: €99 for most long-stay categories, charged in dollars; the student rate is lower and spouses of French nationals pay nothing. Non-refundable whatever the decision.

steps.title: Hand over the passport
steps.detail: It leaves with the file. Ask for the receipt and the tracking reference; nothing that needs the passport can be booked until it is back.

bring: Every document on your list, original plus one copy
Attend the appointment: dossier, biometr.time: About an hour at the centre.
Attend the appointment: dossier, biometr.cost: €99 visa fee (reduced for students, none for spouses of French citizens).

steps.title: Track the file
steps.detail: The TLScontact account shows when the passport is back from the consulate. Two to six weeks is typical; longer in summer or when extra checks are made.

steps.title: Read the sticker before you leave
steps.detail: Your name spelled correctly, the dates covering your move, the number of entries, and the mention: "VLS-TS" means you validate online after arrival; "carte de séjour à solliciter" means a prefecture appointment within two months instead.

steps.title: Copy it
steps.detail: Scan the visa page and the passport photo page; the scans go into the validation and every French office afterwards.

Collect your passport and check the visa.time: Two to six weeks after the appointment.

steps.title: Decide what crosses the ocean
steps.detail: Container shipping is priced by volume and takes six to ten weeks door to door; air freight for a few boxes takes days and costs more per kilo. Most people ship less than they planned.

steps.title: Get three quotes from international movers
steps.detail: Ask for door-to-door including French customs clearance. An inventory in English and French, valued, is required for customs.

steps.title: Claim the duty-free household move
steps.detail: Used personal goods owned for six months or more enter France duty-free when you transfer residence, on presentation of the visa, proof of the old and new addresses and the signed inventory. The mover prepares the customs form.

steps.title: Sell or store the rest
steps.detail: What stays should be sold, given or in storage before the last month; the last month is for the file, not the garage.

bring: Proof of the US and French addresses
Arrange shipping, or sell what stays.time: Quotes in a week; shipping six to ten weeks by sea.
Arrange shipping, or sell what stays.cost: Thousands of dollars for a container; hundreds for boxes by air.

steps.title: Land on or after the visa start date
steps.detail: A day earlier and you enter as a tourist, and the 90-day validation clock is tied to the entry stamp of the correct entry.

steps.title: Fly direct into France if you can
steps.detail: A connection through another Schengen airport means the entry stamp is from that country; it is allowed, but keep the boarding passes to prove the French arrival date.

steps.title: Keep everything
steps.detail: Boarding passes and the e-ticket prove your arrival date for validation if the passport is not stamped.

steps.title: Book the first four to six weeks
steps.detail: Long enough to find a home and receive post. A furnished rental with a proper address (not a hotel room) makes the bank and the validation easier.

steps.title: Get an address you can use
steps.detail: The validation, the bank and the SIM all want a proof of address: the rental agreement or a host's attestation plus their utility bill.

steps.title: Forward the mail
steps.detail: USPS forwards to a US address, not abroad; use a family member or a mail-scanning service and file the change of address online.

steps.title: Fill three months of prescriptions
steps.detail: Carry them in original packaging with the prescription; French pharmacies need a French prescription to refill, so book a doctor early after arrival.

steps.title: Tell the bank and the card issuers
steps.detail: Travel notices, a US address on file, and online banking that works without a US phone.

steps.title: Keep a US number alive
steps.detail: Two-factor codes from US banks, Social Security and the IRS go to a US number. A cheap plan or a number-parking service keeps it.

Tidy the US side: mail, prescriptions, b.cost: Small monthly fees for mail and number services.

steps.title: One folder, in the cabin
steps.detail: Passport with the visa, every apostilled original, the insurance attestation, the accommodation proof, the pet certificate, and a copy of the France-Visas file. Nothing in the hold.

steps.title: Scans in the cloud too
steps.detail: Every page scanned and reachable from your phone; French offices accept uploads and you will be asked for the same documents again and again.

steps.title: Buy a prepaid SIM in the first days
steps.detail: Any carrier shop or supermarket; passport as ID. Move to a contract once you have a French bank account and address.

steps.title: Use the French number everywhere
steps.detail: Bank, ANEF, ameli, the prefecture: every French account sends its codes to a French number.

Get a French SIM.cost: A few euros for the SIM; €10 to €30 a month.

steps.title: Know when they are needed
steps.detail: Not for the consulate, which took your file in English. The prefecture (renewal) and CPAM (health cover) want sworn French translations of the apostilled birth and marriage certificates.

steps.title: Find a traducteur assermenté
steps.detail: Sworn translators are registered as experts with a French cour d'appel; each court publishes its list, and many work from scans by email. Only their stamp counts.

steps.title: Send the full scan
steps.detail: The certificate and its apostille together, front and back. The translation comes back stamped and dated; keep it with the original.

Get sworn French translations.time: A week or two per batch.

steps.title: Go to the ANEF portal
steps.detail: Choose "I validate my VLS-TS". Create an account with your email (activate the link within 24 hours) or sign in with FranceConnect.

steps.title: Enter the visa and the arrival
steps.detail: Visa number, the date you entered France (the entry stamp, not the visa date) and your French address.

steps.title: Upload the proofs
steps.detail: Passport photo page, the visa sticker, and a proof of address in France (lease, rental agreement, or a host attestation with their bill).

steps.title: Pay the validation tax
steps.detail: By card on the portal, or buy the timbre fiscal at timbres.impots.gouv.fr and enter the code the same day. €300 for most categories since May 2026, €150 for students; confirm the amount shown.

steps.title: Save the confirmation
steps.detail: The email and the PDF "confirmation de validation" are your proof of status for the year; the bank, CPAM and the prefecture ask for it.

Validate your visa online within 90 days.time: Half an hour, within 90 days of entry.
Validate your visa online within 90 days.cost: €300 (standard) or €150 (student) validation tax, as of May 2026.

steps.title: Pick a bank that takes newcomers
steps.detail: Traditional banks want an appointment and a proof of address; online banks open in days with a passport and a French address. Being a US citizen adds FATCA paperwork; some banks decline Americans, so ask first.

steps.title: Bring the file
steps.detail: Passport, the visa and its validation confirmation, proof of address (lease or host attestation with bill), and often a US tax number and a proof of income.

steps.title: Get the RIB
steps.detail: The RIB (bank details slip) is what every French service asks for: rent, utilities, CPAM, the phone. The card follows by post in a week or two.

steps.title: Keep the US account
steps.detail: For Social Security, pensions, US cards and the IRS.

steps.title: Build the rental dossier
steps.detail: French landlords ask for a dossier: ID, the visa, proof of income (three months), a tax return or the US equivalent, and often a guarantor. Newcomers without French pay slips offer several months' rent or a guarantee service instead.

steps.title: Look where the listings are
steps.detail: Agencies, the big listing sites, and the mairie's noticeboard in smaller towns. Visits are quick; decisions are the same day in tight markets.

steps.title: Sign, and do the état des lieux
steps.detail: The lease (bail) plus the inventory of condition on entry; photograph everything. The lease becomes your proof of address for every office.

Find permanent housing.cost: Deposit of one month (unfurnished) or two (furnished), plus agency fees.

steps.title: Electricity and gas
steps.detail: Open a contract with any supplier online; you need the meter number (on the meter or the previous bill), the RIB and the move-in date.

steps.title: Water
steps.detail: Often through the commune or a regional company; the landlord or agency says which.

steps.title: Internet and phone
steps.detail: Fibre or ADSL by address; a contract needs a French RIB. Installation takes one to three weeks.

steps.title: Keep the first bills
steps.detail: Each becomes a proof of address for the next office.

steps.title: Start before you need it
steps.detail: The mairie, the local association network and private schools all run classes; the integration contract (CIR) on family routes includes free ones.

steps.title: Aim for A2 then B1
steps.detail: A2 is referenced for some family-route steps; B1 is the citizenship benchmark. Both are ordinary evening-class goals over a year or two.

Enroll in French language classes.cost: Free to a few hundred euros a term.

steps.title: Pick an FBI-approved channeler
steps.detail: A channeler takes your fingerprints electronically and returns the Identity History Summary in days; the FBI's own postal route takes ten to fourteen weeks. The FBI publishes the approved list.

steps.title: Get fingerprinted and submit
steps.detail: Book with the channeler, bring government ID, and ask for the result on FBI letterhead as a PDF and on paper. Some channelers will also arrange the apostille; ask.

steps.title: Apostille it at the US Department of State
steps.detail: A federal document is apostilled by the Office of Authentications in Washington, not by your state. Mail the FBI result with form DS-4194 and the fee, or use the channeler's apostille service.

steps.title: Watch the six-month clock
steps.detail: Consulates want the check issued within six months of your appointment. Count back from the appointment date and order accordingly; too early and you do it twice.

Request your FBI background check.time: Days for the check through a channeler; the federal apostille adds several weeks by mail.
Request your FBI background check.cost: $18 FBI fee plus the channeler's fee, and $20 per document for the federal apostille.

steps.title: Know the benchmark
steps.detail: Consulates measure a visitor against the French net minimum wage, about €1,478 a month in 2026, per adult. Many US applicants show one and a half to two times that in monthly income, or a year's worth in savings, so nobody has to ask.

steps.title: Assemble the proof
steps.detail: Three months of statements for each account, investment balances, pension or Social Security letters, rental income, an employer letter if the income is a salary earned abroad.

steps.title: Write a one-page summary
steps.detail: A simple table: source, monthly amount, where the proof is. Officers read hundreds of files; a summary that matches the statements gets read.

steps.title: Write the attestation sur l'honneur
steps.detail: A short signed statement: "I, [name], born [date], declare on my honour that I will not carry out any professional activity in France during my stay." Dated and signed by each applicant. France-Visas gives the wording for the visitor route.

steps.title: Understand what it covers
steps.detail: Working for a French employer or French clients is out. On remote work for a US employer, the Interior Ministry indicated in a written answer on 23 June 2026 that it may be compatible when the work has no link to the French market; consulates apply this unevenly. Read the visitor guide before you sign, and if it applies to you, say so plainly in the cover letter. The letters in Documents include a remote-work version and an employer letter.

steps.title: Keep your address current
steps.detail: After validation, OFII writes by post or email to the address you validated with. Weeks to months later; moving without telling ANEF means the letter is lost.

steps.title: Attend the medical visit
steps.detail: A chest X-ray and a short screening at the OFII office of your region. Bring the passport, the validation confirmation and the vaccination record if you have one.

steps.title: Family routes: sign the CIR
steps.detail: The integration contract comes with a language assessment and civics days; attendance counts at renewal.

steps.title: Wait three months of residence
steps.detail: Cover on the residence criterion opens after three months of stable, regular residence for those not working; workers are covered from the first payslip.

steps.title: Fill in form 736
steps.detail: The "demande d'affiliation au régime général sur critère de résidence", from ameli.fr, sent to the CPAM of your département by post or through your ameli account once you have one.

steps.title: Attach the file
steps.detail: Passport and visa with the validation confirmation, proof of address, birth certificate with a sworn French translation, a RIB, and a proof of income or a statement of no income.

steps.title: Wait for the number
steps.detail: A provisional social security number first, then the permanent one; the carte Vitale is requested once the number is permanent. Keep paying and keeping receipts meanwhile.

Apply for French health cover (PUMa).time: Weeks to months after the file is complete.
Apply for French health cover (PUMa).cost: Free; a means-tested contribution may apply to high capital income.

steps.title: Count four months back from the expiry date
steps.detail: Renewal is filed between four and two months before the VLS-TS expires, online through ANEF for most categories. Late filing after expiry costs a €180 surcharge and leaves you without status.

steps.title: Rebuild the file
steps.detail: Passport, the current visa and validation, proof of address, proof of resources for the year, insurance or health cover, the sworn translations of your civil records, photos. The prefecture's page lists the exact set for your card.

steps.title: Keep the récépissé
steps.detail: The receipt keeps you legal while the card is made; prefecture delays are the usual bottleneck.

Start the renewal four months before the.time: File four months out; the card takes months.
Start the renewal four months before the.cost: Stamp duty on the card, set annually.

steps.title: Wait for the permanent number
steps.detail: The card is requested once CPAM has issued the permanent social security number; ameli sends the request or you do it in your ameli account.

steps.title: Send the photo and the ID
steps.detail: A passport-style photo and a copy of your ID, online or on the paper form.

steps.title: Use the attestation meanwhile
steps.detail: The attestation de droits from your ameli account works at the doctor and the pharmacy until the card arrives.

Get Carte Vitale.time: Weeks to months after the number.

steps.title: Know the calendar
steps.detail: The French return covers the calendar year and is filed the following spring (April to June). Your first one covers the year you arrived, from the arrival date.

steps.title: Get a tax number
steps.detail: A first return is filed on paper (form 2042) at your local tax office, which then issues the numéro fiscal for online filing the year after.

steps.title: Declare worldwide income and foreign accounts
steps.detail: US income goes on the return with the treaty credits; every foreign bank account is listed on form 3916. This is the return a cross-border professional should prepare, at least the first time.

steps.title: Keep filing in the US
steps.detail: The US return and the FBAR continue. The two returns are prepared together.

File French tax return.cost: Professional fees if you use one.

steps.title: Find someone who does both countries
steps.detail: A US CPA or enrolled agent who prepares French returns too, or a French expert-comptable with US clients. Ask how many US-French clients they file for each year.

steps.title: Bring the whole picture
steps.detail: Every income source, every account, retirement plans, property in both countries, the move date, and the visa route. The year you become French tax resident is the year to plan.

steps.title: Decide the move date with them
steps.detail: Where in the year you arrive changes the first French return and the US foreign earned income and credit positions.

Talk to a cross-border tax professional.time: One or two meetings before the move.
Talk to a cross-border tax professional.cost: Hundreds to low thousands of dollars.

steps.title: List every account and benefit
steps.detail: Social Security, private pensions, IRAs, 401(k)s, Roth accounts, annuities.

steps.title: Ask the treaty questions
steps.detail: Which are taxed only in the US under the treaty, which France taxes with a credit, how Roth withdrawals are treated, and what the French return needs to show so the treaty applies.

steps.title: Plan withdrawals around it
steps.detail: Timing distributions before or after the move can change the bill; decide with the professional, not after.

steps.title: Check the list once more
steps.detail: North Carolina has no reciprocal agreement as of September 2026. If that changes before your first year ends, the exchange is the easier path.

steps.title: Get an International Driving Permit before you leave
steps.detail: From AAA in the US; it carries the French translation of your licence for the first year, when your US licence is still valid.

steps.title: Register: driving school or candidat libre
steps.detail: An auto-école handles the paperwork, lessons and exam bookings (roughly €1,200 to €3,800, at least 20 hours of lessons in most areas). Candidat libre means registering yourself on ANTS and booking exams directly, cheaper and slower.

steps.title: Pass the code de la route
steps.detail: Forty questions at an approved centre, about €30. The exam is in French; the vocabulary is limited and learnable.

steps.title: Pass the practical
steps.detail: Booked through the school or ANTS, €32 to €50 depending on the prefecture; waits for a slot run weeks to months. On passing, a provisional certificate, then the card, with a three-year probation and a lower alcohol limit.

steps.title: Do it inside the first year
steps.detail: After a year of residence an unexchanged US licence is no longer valid in France. Start in the first months.

Pass the French driving test before your.time: Months; start early in the first year.
Pass the French driving test before your.cost: €1,200 to €3,800 through a school; exam fees on top.

steps.title: Order a certified copy
steps.detail: From the state or county where the licence was issued; the CDC directory names the office and whether it is state or county.

steps.title: Apostille it at that state's Secretary of State
steps.detail: The NASS directory has the office, fee and turnaround. Send the certified copy with the request form naming France; keep the apostille attached when it returns.

steps.title: Scan it
steps.detail: Front and back, apostille included; the scan is what the translator and French offices use later.

links.label: Where to write for vital records (CDC)

steps.title: After arrival, not for the consulate
steps.detail: The consulate takes the certificate in English; the prefecture and CPAM want a sworn French translation.

steps.title: Use a traducteur assermenté
steps.detail: Registered with a French cour d'appel; works from a scan of the apostilled certificate.

steps.title: Build Sam's dossier in parallel
steps.detail: Their own passport, photos, France-Visas form, proof of accommodation, insurance attestation, financial proof (shared accounts are fine, named on both), and their own certified, apostilled birth certificate.

steps.title: One appointment, two files
steps.detail: Book consecutive TLScontact slots; each file is judged on its own.

steps.title: A separate France-Visas application
steps.detail: In Sam's name, same route and dates as yours.

steps.title: Same TLScontact day
steps.detail: Consecutive slots; the fee is per applicant.

steps.title: Wait the same three months
steps.detail: Residence-based cover opens for each adult separately after three months of stable residence; there is no dependant status for a spouse.

steps.title: File form 736 in Sam's name
steps.detail: The same form as yours, sent to the same CPAM, with Sam's passport and visa, validation confirmation, proof of the shared address, their apostilled birth certificate with a sworn translation, and a RIB (a joint account is fine).

steps.title: Two numbers, two cards
steps.detail: Each of you gets a social security number and, later, a carte Vitale.

Register spouse for social security.time: After three months of residence; weeks to months to process.
